speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on achieving our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and stable prices for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Although important federal government data for the past couple of months have yet to be released, available public- and private-sector data suggest that the outlook for employment and inflation has not changed much since our meeting in October.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Conditions in the labor market appear to be gradually cooling, and inflation remains somewhat elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In support of our goals, and in light of the balance of risks to employment and inflation, today the Federal Open Market Committee decided to lower our policy interest rate by ¼ percentage point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As a separate matter, we also decided to initiate purchases of shorter-term Treasury securities solely for the purpose of maintaining an ample supply of reserves over time, thus supporting effective control of our policy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will have more to say about monetary policy and its implementation after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Although some key government data have yet to be released, available indicators suggest that economic activity has been expanding at a moderate pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Consumer spending appears to have remained solid, and business fixed investment has continued to expand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In contrast, activity in the housing sector remains weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The temporary shutdown of the federal government has likely weighed on economic activity in the current quarter, but these effects should be mostly offset by higher growth next quarter, reflecting the reopening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our Summary of Economic Projections, the median participant projects that real GDP will rise 1.7 percent this year and 2.3 percent next year, somewhat stronger than projected in September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the labor market, although official employment data for October and November are delayed, available evidence suggests that both layoffs and hiring remain low, and that both households’ perceptions of job availability and firms’ perceptions of hiring difficulty continue to decline.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The official report on the labor market for September, the most recent release, showed that the unemployment rate continued to edge up, reaching 4.4 percent, and that job gains had slowed significantly since earlier in the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A good part of the slowing likely reflects a decline in the growth of the labor force due to lower immigration and labor force participation, though labor demand has clearly softened as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In this less dynamic and somewhat softer labor market, the downside risks to employment appear to have risen in recent months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our SEP, the median projection of the unemployment rate is 4.5 percent at the end of this year and edges down thereafter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased significantly from its highs in mid-2022 but remains somewhat elevated relative to our 2 percent longer-run goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Very little data on inflation have been released since our meeting in October.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Total PCE prices rose 2.8 percent over the 12 months ending in September, and, excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices also rose 2.8 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These readings are higher than earlier in the year, as inflation for goods has picked up, reflecting the effects of tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In contrast, disinflation appears to be continuing for services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Near-term measures of inflation expectations have declined from their peaks earlier in the year, as reflected in both market- and survey-based measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Most measures of longer-term expectations remain consistent with our 2 percent inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median projection in the SEP for total PCE inflation is 2.9 percent this year and 2.4 percent next year, a bit lower than the median projection in September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thereafter, the median falls to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our monetary policy actions are guided by our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At today’s meeting, the Committee decided to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by ¼ percentage point to 3½ to 3¾ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the near term, risks to inflation are tilted to the upside and risks to employment to the downside—a challenging situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There is no risk-free path for policy as we navigate this tension between our employment and inflation goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A reasonable base case is that the effects of tariffs on inflation will be relatively short lived—effectively a one-time shift in the price level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our obligation is to make sure that a one-time increase in the price level does not become an ongoing inflation problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, with downside risks to employment having risen in recent months, the balance of risks has shifted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our framework calls for us to take a balanced approach in promoting both sides of our dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Accordingly, we judged it appropriate at this meeting to lower our policy rate by ¼ percentage point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: With today’s decision, we have lowered our policy rate ¾ percentage point over our last three meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This further normalization of our policy stance should help stabilize the labor market while allowing inflation to resume its downward trend toward 2 percent once the effects of tariffs have passed through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The adjustments to our policy stance since September bring it within a range of plausible estimates of neutral and leave us well positioned to determine the extent and timing of additional adjustments to our policy rate based on the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our Summary of Economic Projections, FOMC participants wrote down their individual assessments of an appropriate path of the federal funds rate under what each participant judges to be the most likely scenario for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median participant projects that the appropriate level of the federal funds rate will be 3.4 percent at the end of 2026 and 3.1 percent at the end of 2027, unchanged from September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As is always the case, these individual forecasts are subject to uncertainty, and they are not a Committee plan or decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Monetary policy is not on a preset course, and we will make our decisions on a meeting-by-meeting basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Let me turn now to issues related to the implementation of monetary policy, with the reminder that these issues are separate from—and have no implications for—the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In light of the continued tightening in money market interest rates relative to our administered rates, and other indicators of reserve market conditions, the Committee judged that reserve balances have declined to ample levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Accordingly, at today’s meeting, the Committee decided to initiate purchases of shorter-term Treasury securities—mainly Treasury bills—for the sole purpose of maintaining an ample supply of reserves over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Such increases in our securities holdings ensure that the federal funds rate remains within its target range and are necessary because the growth of the economy leads to rising demand over time for our liabilities, including currency and reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As detailed in a statement released today by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, reserve management purchases will amount to $40 billion in the first month and may remain elevated for a few months to alleviate expected near-term pressures in money markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thereafter, we expect the size of reserve management purchases to decline, though the actual pace will depend on market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our implementation framework, an ample supply of reserves means that the federal funds rate and other short-term interest rates are primarily controlled by the setting of our administered rates rather than day-to-day discretionary interventions in money markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In this regime, standing repurchase agreement, or repo, operations are a critical tool to ensure that the federal funds rate remains within its target range, even on days of elevated pressures in money markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Consistent with this view, the Committee eliminated the aggregate limit on standing repo operations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These operations are intended to support monetary policy implementation and smooth market functioning and should be used when economically sensible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: To conclude: The Fed has been assigned two goals for monetary policy: maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to supporting maximum employment, bringing inflation sustainably to our 2 percent goal, and keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our success in delivering on these goals matters to all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the Fed, we will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I look forward to your questions.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Howard.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Howard Schneider, with Reuters.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Just first turning to the statement, just to be clear we’re on the same page here, the insertion of the phrase “In considering the extent and timing of additional adjustments”—does that indicate that the Fed is now on hold until there’s some clearer signal from inflation or jobs or the evolution of the economy along the baseline outlook?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, yes, the adjustments since September bring our policy within a broad range of estimates of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And as we noted in our statement today, we are well positioned to determine the extent and timing of additional adjustments based on the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That new language points out that we’ll carefully evaluate that incoming data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, also, I would note that having reduced our policy rate by 75 basis points since September and 175 basis points since last September, the fed funds rate is now within a broad range of estimates of its neutral value, and we are well positioned to wait to see how the economy evolves.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: And if I could follow up on the outlook there: It seems like with the additional GDP growth coupled with easing inflation and a fairly steady unemployment rate, this seems like a pretty optimistic outlook for next year.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: What’s given rise to that?

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Is this an early bet on AI?

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Is there some sense of improving productivity out there?

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: What’s driving that?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So a number of things are driving what’s happening in the forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I would say, if you look broadly at outside forecasts, you do see a pickup in growth in many of those now, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it is—it’s partly that consumer spending has held up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s been resilient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: To another degree, it is that AI—spending on data centers and related to AI has been holding up business investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, overall, the baseline expectation for next year is, at least at the Fed and I think with outside forecasters, too, is a pickup in growth from today’s relatively low level of 1.7 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mentioned that the SEP median is 1.7 for this year—growth—and 2.3 for next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yet actually—some of that is due to the shutdown.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you can take two-tenths out of 2026 and put it in 2025.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it would really be 1.9 and 2.1.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, overall, yes, you know, for a few reasons.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Fiscal policy is going to be supportive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, as I mentioned, AI spending will continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The consumer continues to spend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it looks like the baseline would be solid growth next year.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Steve.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Thank you, Mr. Chairman, for taking our questions here.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: You had previously described rate cuts in terms of a risk-management framework.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: And, kind of following up on what Howard was asking, is the risk-management phase of rate cuts over here, and have you taken out sufficient insurance, I guess, against potential weakness in terms of the data we might get next week when it comes to employment?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re going to get a great deal of data between now and the January meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I’m sure we’ll talk more about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that will—the data that we get are going to factor into our thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, yes, we have—if you go back, we held our policy rate at, you know, 5.4 percent for more than a year because inflation was high, very high, and unemployment—and the labor market was really solid at that point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So what happened is, over last summer—summer of ’24—inflation came down and the labor market began to show real signs of weakness.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we decided, as our framework tells us to do, that when the risks to the two goals become more equal, you should move from a stance that favors really dealing with one of them—in that case, inflation—to a more balanced, more neutral setting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we did that, and we did some cutting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then we paused for a while to work our way through what was happening in the middle of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then we resumed cuts in September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ve cut now three—we’ve now cut a total of 175 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, as I mentioned, you know, we feel like where we’re positioned now puts—we’re well positioned to wait and see how the economy evolves from here.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: If I could just follow up on the SEP. You have a whole lot of—big increase in the growth numbers, but not a big decline in the unemployment numbers.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: And is that an AI factor in there?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: What is going on in terms of the dynamic of you get more growth, but you don’t get a whole lot of decline in unemployment?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Thank you, sir.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it is—the implication is obviously higher productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And some of that may be AI.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It just—also, I think productivity has just been almost structurally higher for several years now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if you start thinking of it as 2 percent per year, you can sustain higher growth without more job creation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course, higher productivity is also what enables incomes to rise over long periods of time, so it’s basically a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that may be—that’s certainly the implication.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Colby.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Colby Smith with the New York Times.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Today’s decision was clearly very divided.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: It wasn’t just the two official dissents against the cut, but there were also soft dissents from four others.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: And I’m just wondering if this reluctance from several people to support recent reductions suggests that there is a much higher bar for cuts in the near term, and what exactly does the Committee need to see if things are well positioned right now to support a January reduction?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So let me just say, as I mentioned—and as I’ve mentioned here before—the situation is that our two goals are a bit in tension, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, interestingly, everyone around the table at the FOMC agrees that inflation is too high and that we want it to come down and agrees that the labor market has softened and that there’s further risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everyone agrees on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Where the difference is is, how do you weight those risks and what does your forecast look like and where do—ultimately, where do you think the bigger risk is?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, it’s very unusual to have persistent tension between the two parts of the mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And when you do, this is what you see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think it’s actually what you would expect to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we do see it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Meanwhile, the discussions we have are as good as any we’ve had in my 14 years at the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re very thoughtful, respectful.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you just have people who have strong views.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we come together and we reach—we reach, you know, a place where we can make a decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We made a decision today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We had—you know, 9 out of 12 supported it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So fairly broad support.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s not like the normal situation where everyone agrees on the direction and what to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s more—it’s more spread out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think that’s only inherent in the situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of what it would take, you know, we all have an outlook in terms of what’s going to come, but I think, ultimately, having cut 75 and, you know, the effects of the 75 basis points will only begin to be coming in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I’ve said before a couple of times, we’re well positioned to wait to see how the economy evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll just have to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we will get, as you know, quite a bit of data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I should mention on the data, as long as I’m talking about it, that we’re going to need to be careful in assessing particularly the household survey data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are very technical reasons about the way data are collected in some of these measures, both in, you know, inflation and in labor—in the labor market, so that the data may be distorted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And not just sort of more volatile, but distorted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s—and that’s really because data was not collected in October and half of November.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re going to get data, but we’re going to have to look at it carefully and with a somewhat skeptical eye by the time of the January meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Notwithstanding that, we will have a lot of the December data by the time of the January meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we expect to see a lot more, but I’m just saying that the—what we get for, for example, CPI or for the, you know, household survey, we’re going to look—we’re going to look at that really carefully and understand that it may be distorted by very technical factors.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: And just one more question on dissents.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: I mean, you talk about it in a very positive way just given the complicated nature of the situation we’re in economically.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: But is there any point in which those dissents become counterproductive either to, you know, the Fed’s communication and the messaging around the policy path forward?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t—I don’t feel that we’re at that point at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would say, again, these are good, thoughtful, respectful discussions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you hear people say—and you’ll hear many outside analysts say the same thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I could make a case for either side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, I could make that case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a close call.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have to make decisions, and we—you know, we always hope that the data will give us a clear read.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But in this situation, you have competing—if you look—if you look through the SEP, you’ll see that a very large number of participants agree that risks are to the upside for unemployment and to the upside for inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So what do you do?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ve got one tool.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can’t do two things at once.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So at what pace do you move?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: How, how—what size moves do you make and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And what’s the timing of them?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s very—it’s a very challenging situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we’re in a good place to, as I mentioned, to wait and see how the economy evolves.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Nick.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Nick Timiraos of the Wall Street Journal.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Chair Powell, there’s been some discussion recently of the 1990s.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: In the 1990s, the Committee did two discrete sequences of three quarter-point cuts, one in 1995–96 and one in 1998.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: And after both of those, the next move in rates was up, not down.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: With policy now closer to neutral, is it a foregone conclusion that the next move in rates is down, or should we think of policy risks as genuinely two-sided from here?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I don’t think that a rate hike is anybody’s base as the next thing—is anybody’s base case at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I’m not hearing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What you see is some people feel we should stop here and that we’re at the right place and just wait.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Some people feel like we should cut once or more this year and next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the—but when people are writing down their estimates of policy of where it should go, it is either holding here or cutting a little or cutting more than a little.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I don’t see that as—I don’t see the base case as involving that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, of course, you know, a data set of two, now three, is not a big data set.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But you are right about those two three-cut times in the ’90s.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: If I could follow up: The unemployment rate has been rising very gradually for the better part of two years.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: And, indeed, the statement today no longer describes the unemployment rate as remaining low.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: What gives you confidence it won’t continue rising in 2026, especially when housing and other rate-sensitive sectors still appear to be feeling restrictive policy from the—notwithstanding the 150 basis points in cuts prior to today?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, yeah, the idea is that with now having cut 75 basis points more now and having policy, you know, I’d call it in a broad range of plausible estimates of neutral, that that will be a place which will enable the labor market to stabilize or to only kick up one or two more tenths.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we won’t see, you know, any kind of a sharper downturn, which we haven’t seen any evidence of at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, policy is still in a place where it’s not accommodative, and we feel like—we feel like we have made progress this year in nontariff-related inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And as tariffs come through, as they flow through, that’ll show through next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, as I said, we’re well past—well placed to wait and see how that turns out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That is our expectation, but, you know, we’re going to start to see the data, and it’ll tell us whether we were right or not.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Claire.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Claire Jones, Financial Times.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: A lot of people interpreted your comments at the October meeting that, you know, when there’s a foggy situation we slow down to mean that, you know, there won’t be a cut now, there’ll be a cut in January instead.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: So it’d be good to get a sense of why did the Committee decide to move today rather than to move in January instead.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So in October, I said that there was no certainty of moving.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that was indeed correct.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I said it’s possible you could think about it that way, but I was careful to say other people could look at it differently.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So why did we move today?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I would say—point to a couple of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: First of all, gradual cooling in the labor market has continued.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Unemployment is now up three-tenths from June through September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Payroll jobs averaging 40,000 per month since April.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think there’s an overstatement in these numbers by about 60,000, so that would be negative 20,000 per month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And also, just to point out one other thing, surveys of households and businesses both showed declining supply and demand for workers, so I think you can say that the labor market has continued to cool gradually, maybe just a touch more gradually than we thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, in terms of inflation, we are—it’s come in a touch lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think the evidence is kind of growing that what’s happening here is services inflation coming down, and that’s offset by increases in goods, and that goods inflation is entirely in sectors where there are tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that does build on the story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so far, it’s only a story that this is—that the goods inflation, which is really the source of the excess at this point, that that—almost more than half the source of the excess inflation is goods—is tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you’ve got to say then, “So what do we expect from tariffs?” And it’s—I would say that is, to some extent, down to looking for broader economic, you know, heat.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, do we see a hot economy?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Do we see constraints?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Do we see what’s going on with wages?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You saw the ECI report today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It doesn’t feel like a hot economy that wants to generate, you know, a Phillips curve kind of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we look at all those things, and we say that this was a decision to make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Obviously, it wasn’t unanimous.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, overall, that was the judgment that we made, and that’s the action we took.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Just on the ample-reserves point, how concerned were people around the table about some of the tensions we’ve seen in money markets?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, I wouldn’t say “concerned.” So what really happened is this: Balance sheet shrinkage, sometimes called QT, went on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We had a framework in place for monitoring it, and nothing happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The overnight reverse repo facility went down pretty much close to zero.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then, beginning in mid-September, the federal funds rate started to tick up within the range, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it ticked up almost all the way to interest on reserve balances.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s nothing wrong with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What that’s telling you is that we’re actually in a reserves—in an ample-reserves regime.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, we knew this was going to come.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: When it finally did come, it came a little quicker than expected, but we were, yeah, absolutely there to take the actions that we said we would take.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And those actions are today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, we announced that we’re resuming reserve management purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That is completely separate from monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just we need to keep an ample supply of reserves out there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Why so big?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The answer to that is, you know, if you look ahead, you will see that April 15th is coming up, and our framework is such that we want to have ample reserves even at times when reserves are at a low level temporarily.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what happens on Tax Day.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: People pay a lot of money to the government, reserves drop sharply and temporarily.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So this seasonal buildup that we’ll see in the next few months was going to happen anyway.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It was going to happen because April 15th is April 15th.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s also a secular ongoing growth of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have to keep reserves, call it, constant as a—as it relates to the banking system or to the whole economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that alone calls for us to increase about $20 [or] $25 billion per month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s a small part.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s also happening in the context of a temporary few month front-loading to get reserves high enough to get through the, you know, the tax period in mid-April.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what’s happening there.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Andrew.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Thanks, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: This is the last post-FOMC press conference before an important Supreme Court hearing next month.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Can you talk about how you’re hoping the Supreme Court will rule?

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: And I’m just curious why the Fed’s been so reticent on such a pivotal matter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not something I want to address here, Andrew.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’re not legal commentators.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s before the courts, and we think our—we don’t think that we help matters by trying to engage as a public discussant of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll give you a mulligan, though.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Thanks.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: I don’t know if that means I get three questions, but— CHAIR POWELL.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: No, just one, just one more.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: [Laughter] ANDREW ACKERMAN.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: I guess I wanted to come back to the 1990s question.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Like, do you see that as a useful model for thinking about what is happening in the economy right now?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t think it rises to that level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I did think that in 2019, when we cut three times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, this is such a unique situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is—it’s not the 1970s, let’s put it that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we do have tension between our two goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so that’s just unique in my time at the Fed and I think going back a long ways.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We haven’t had that in our framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our framework, as you know, says that when that’s the case, that we try to, you know, take a balanced approach to the two things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We look at how far they are and how long it would take to get them back to—each of them back to the goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s a very subjective analysis, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it just tells you you’ve got to—and I think, ultimately, what it says is, when they’re broadly equally threatened or equally at risk, you should be kind of neutral because if you’re either accommodative or tight, you’re favoring one or the other goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we’ve been trying to—we’ve been sort of moving in the direction of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now we’re in the range of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re in the high end of the range of neutral, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s what we’re doing now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It so happened that we’ve cut three times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we haven’t made any decision about January.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, as I’ve said, we think we’re well positioned to wait and see how the economy performs.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Edward.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Thanks, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Edward Lawrence, with Fox Business.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: I wanted to ask you, the inflation expectations has come down in your SEP report.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Do you see the tariff price increases as passing through in the next three months?

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Is it a six-month process that we’re looking for that to end?

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: And then, because of that, is jobs the threat to the economy?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So with tariff inflation, you know, it takes—there’s the announcement of a tariff and then there’s—you know, they start to take effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then it takes some months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Goods may have to be shipped from other parts of the—you know, it may take, you know, quite a while for an individual tariff to take its full effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But once it’s had that effect, then the question is, isn’t that just a one-time price increase?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ve actually—we actually look at all of the announcements.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And what you get from all that, you see sort of a—for each one of them, there’s a time period and then it’s fully in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if there are no new tariff announcements—and we don’t know that, but let’s assume there are no major new tariff announcements—inflation from goods should peak in the first quarter or so, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Or roughly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we haven’t been able to predict this with any precision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No one is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But call it the first quarter or so of next year should be the peak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And from here, it should be—it shouldn’t be big, it should be a couple tenths or even less than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t really have precision on this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, after that, again, if there are no new tariffs that are being announced that will take nine months to get fully in—and nine months is also an estimate—then you should start to see that coming down in the back half of next year.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: And I wanted to see if I could address sort of the elephant in the room.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: The President’s been talking openly about a new Fed Chairman.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Does that hinder your current job right now or change your thinking at all?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Mike.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: No mulligans for Ed.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: [Laughter] Michael McKee from Bloomberg Radio and Television.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Ten-year rates have—are 50 basis points higher than when you started cutting back in September of 2024, and the yield curve basically has been steepening.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Why do you think that continuing to cut now, especially in the absence of data, is going to bring down the yield on the thing that will move the economy the most?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re looking at the real economy and focusing on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you have—you’ve got—when the long bonds move around, you’ve got to look at why they’re moving around.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look at inflation compensation, it’s very—that’s one part of it is inflation compensation breakevens, and, you know, they’re at very comfortable levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re at levels consistent—past—once you get out past the very short term now, breakevens are at a, you know, at quite—levels that are quite consistent with 2 percent inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there’s nothing happening with rates going up out there that suggests concern about inflation in the long term or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, I look at these things pretty regularly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Same thing with surveys.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Surveys are all saying that the public understands our commitment to 2 percent and expects us to get back there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So why are rates going up?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It has to be something else.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It must be, you know, an expectation of higher growth or something like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s a lot of what’s been going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, you saw a big move, you know, toward the end of last year, which was not to do with us, it was to do with other developments.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Well, you just mentioned that we’re—the public is expecting you to get back to 2 percent.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: And Americans, overwhelmingly, are citing high prices, inflation, as their number one concern.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Can you explain to them why you’re prioritizing the labor market, which seems relatively stable to most people, instead of their number-one concern, inflation?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we—as you know, we have a network of contacts in the U.S. economy which is really unmatched if you go through the 12 Reserve Banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we hear loud and clear how people are experiencing, really, costs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s really high costs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And a lot of that is not the current rate of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A lot of that is just embedded higher cost due to higher inflation in 2022 and ’23.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what’s going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so the best thing we can do is restore inflation to its 2 percent goal—and our policy is intended to do that—but also have a strong economy where real wages are going up, where people are getting jobs and earning money.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And they’re—we’re going to need to have some years where real compensation is higher, you know, it’s positive, significantly positive, so wages—nominal wages are higher than inflation for people to start feeling good about affordability—the affordability issue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, so we’re working hard on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We want to—we’re trying to keep inflation under control but also support the labor market and strong wages so that people are earning enough money and feeling economically healthy again.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Victoria.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Hi.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Victoria Guida with Politico.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Just to follow up on that, I mean, this is now the third time that you’ve cut this year, and inflation is around 3 percent.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: So is the message that you’re sort of trying to send with that that you’re okay with where inflation is for now as long as people understand that, at some point, you still want to get back to 2 percent because inflation is relatively stable where it is?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everyone should understand, and the surveys show that they do, that we’re committed to 2 percent inflation and we will deliver 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s a complicated, unusual, difficult situation where the labor market is also under pressure, where job creation may actually be negative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, supply of workers has also gone way down, so the unemployment rate hasn’t moved that much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, it’s a labor market that seems to have significant downside risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: People care a lot about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s their jobs, that’s their ability, if they get laid off or if they’re entering the labor force, to find work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s really important to people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The story with inflation—and, you know, we’re well aware that this is a story at this point—is that if you get away from tariffs, inflation is in the low 2s, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s really tariffs that’s causing the—most of the inflation overshoot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we do think of those as likely to, in the current situation, as likely to be a one-time, you know, one-time price increase.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our job is to make sure that it is, and we will do that job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, right now, you’ve got this difficult balance, and there are risks to both sides.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s no risk-free path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If we were—if we—you know, if it was just inflation and the labor market was just really strong and then we’d—rates would be higher, as they were for more than a year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we didn’t have to worry about inflation—sorry, about the labor market, because the labor market, unemployment was very low, if you remember, when inflation was very high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There was a labor shortage, so we could focus entirely on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now it’s different.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We actually have risks to both.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think we’re doing the best we can for people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They also care about their jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They do care about affordability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the best thing we can do there is both to support economic activity but also, you know, make sure that when tariff inflation goes down and disappears, inflation lands around 2 percent.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Elizabeth.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Thanks so much.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Elizabeth Schulze, with ABC News.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Just to follow up, you keep talking about job growth being negative.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Why do you think job growth is so much worse than all the official data?

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Why do you think job growth is—to follow up on your comments about job growth, why is it so much worse than the official data is suggesting?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Oh, well, we just—we know, I think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s, it’s—this is—I don’t think this is particularly controversial.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s a—it’s very difficult to estimate job growth in real time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They don’t count everybody.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They have a survey.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And there’s been something of a systematic overcount.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we expect it and they correct it twice a year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the last time they corrected it, we thought the correction would be 800,000 or 900,000.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I won’t get the numbers exactly right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that was exactly what happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we think that that has persisted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so there was an overcount in the payroll job numbers, we think, continuing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it will be corrected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t have the exact month in my head right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But—and that’s just—I don’t—again, I think forecasters generally understand that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—and we think it’s about 60,000 a month, so 40,000 jobs could be negative 20.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, that could be wrong by 10 or 20 in either direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, in any case—but the thing is, that’s, that’s job creation, in a way, that’s demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Labor supply has also come down quite sharply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, if you had a world where they’re just—there’s just no growth in workers and you really don’t need a lot of jobs to have full employment, some people argue that’s what we’re looking at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I think a world where job creation is negative, I just think we need to watch that situation very carefully and be in a position where we’re not, you know, pushing down on job creation with our policy.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: When we’re talking about supply, we have seen major American employers like Amazon cite AI in job cuts.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: How much right now are you factoring in AI into the current weakness in the job market?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s probably part of the story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not a big part of the story yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know whether it will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, for example, if you look at—you can’t miss the big announcements of layoffs and also companies saying that they’re not going to hire anybody for a long time, and they cite AI—that’s all clearly happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, people are not filing for unemployment insurance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And since job creation—job-finding rates are extremely low, if there were big numbers of layoffs, you’d expect the continuing claims to go up, and you’d expect new claims to go up, but they really haven’t much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s a little bit curious.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But longer term, though, you know, the question is, what are we going to see here?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s—you know, there’s a—it may be that, in past technology, really significant technology and innovation eras, you have seen some jobs destroyed and other jobs made.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Ultimately, what’s happened for a couple hundred years is, when you get through all that, you have higher productivity, and you have new jobs, and there are enough jobs for people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is a—this may be different.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s—every time we have a wave of technology, we think, “Oh, this could put a lot of people out of work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What are they going to do?” In the past, there’s always been more work and higher productivity, and incomes have risen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What will happen here?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re going to have to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But right now is such early days, we don’t think we see much—it’s certainly not showing up in layoffs yet.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Enda.

speaker: ENDA CURRAN
sentence: Thank you, Chair.

speaker: ENDA CURRAN
sentence: Enda Curran, Bloomberg News.

speaker: ENDA CURRAN
sentence: Given the breadth of views on the policy Committee, why is there such a division of views between the— CHAIR POWELL.

speaker: ENDA CURRAN
sentence: On the policy what?

speaker: ENDA CURRAN
sentence: On the Committee.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: ENDA CURRAN
sentence: Why is there such a division of views between the presidents and the Board members?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s not so stark as that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The views are more varied on each—in each group as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s some of that, but I would say there are also Governors and there are people in both—on both sides in both groups.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I wouldn’t put too much in that.

speaker: ENDA CURRAN
sentence: Okay.

speaker: ENDA CURRAN
sentence: And just to follow up, given your growth upgrade, how would you factor in or what would be the economic impact if the Supreme Court is to strike down the tariffs that they’re currently hearing in terms of growth and inflation?

speaker: ENDA CURRAN
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I really don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It would depend on—it would depend on a whole bunch of things we don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I can’t really help you there.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Christine.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: Thank you, Chair Powell.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: Christine Romans, NBC News.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: I wanted to ask you about how the higher-income households are really driving spending right now.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: They’re backed by home equity and stock market wealth.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: But lower-income consumers are really struggling with the accumulation of five years now of rising prices.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: It’s price levels, not really the inflation rate, holding some of these families back.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: How sustainable is this so-called K-shaped economy?

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: And what are the Fed’s thoughts on whether that’s a risk going forward?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we do, through our vast network of contacts and just through our observation of what’s going on in the economy, we hear about this a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you listen to the earnings reports for consumer-facing companies that tend to deal with low- and moderate-income people, they’ll all say that we’re seeing people, you know, tightening their belts, you know, changing products that they buy, buying less and that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so it’s clearly a thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s also clearly a thing that, you know, asset values, housing values, and securities values are high, and they tend to be owned by people more at the higher end of the income and wealth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so, as to how sustainable it is, I don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Most of the consumption does happen by people who have more means.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think, you know, the top third accounts for way more than a third of the consumption, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s a good question how sustainable that is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, the best we can do is to have, you know, price stability and a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And what we saw—for example, what we saw at the end of the, you know, the very, very long expansion that ended with the outbreak of the pandemic, we saw that it was 10 years and 8 months or something like that—the longest one in recorded history.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the last two years, most of the job—the largest part of the wage gains were going to people in the bottom quartile, the bottom part of the low and moderate income.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, having a strong labor market for a long period of time is really, really good from a social standpoint.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s helping people at the lower-income levels, and that’s what we all want to get back to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we’ve got to have price stability, and we’ve got to have, you know, full employment, maximum employment.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: And, just quickly, you mentioned the housing market remains kind of weak.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: With these rate cuts that we’ve seen, is there a chance we’re going to see more affordability in the housing market so more people can maybe enjoy that part of wealth creation?

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: I mean, the average age—the median age of a first-time homebuyer is now 40 years old.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: That’s the highest on record.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, so the housing market faces some really significant challenges.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I don’t know that, you know, a 25 basis point decline in the federal funds rate is going to make much of a difference for people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, housing supply is low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Many people have very, very low-rate mortgages from the pandemic period, and they kept refinancing and caught the really low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s made it expensive for them to move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we’re a ways away from that changing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Also, we’re just—we haven’t built enough housing in the country for a long time, and so a lot of estimates suggest that we just need more housing of different kinds.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So housing is going to be a, you know, a problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, really the tools to address it are—we can raise and lower interest rates, but we don’t really have the tools to address, you know, a secular housing shortage—a structural housing shortage.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Chris.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Thanks.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Chris Rugaber, Associated Press.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: You mentioned on inflation services inflation being low, goods inflation looking like maybe it’ll peak.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: We had the wages report you mentioned today showing moderating wage growth.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Where are the inflation risks?

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: It looks like inflation is cooling in your view.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: At the same time, you have potentially negative hiring.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Why not—why aren’t we hearing more about maybe more cuts in this environment?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, I think the risk of inflation is pretty clear to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that is, you know, we see higher inflation, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Most of the inflation over target is from goods.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we think, we estimate, we expect—most of us—that inflation will be a one-time price increase and then come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We just came off an experience where inflation turned out to be much more persistent than anyone had expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Is that going to happen now?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, that’s—so that’s the risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The risk is either that tariff inflation just turns out to be more and more persistent, maybe because companies who are now holding back from passing through the tariffs will just keep doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’ll see—you see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think the other possibility is less likely, and that is just that, you know, the labor market gets tight or the economy gets tight and you see, you know, just traditional inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t see that as particularly likely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But—so I think—you know, again, you know, all across the Committee, people see the picture pretty similarly but see the risks quite differently.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And some people do see the inflation risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I wouldn’t dismiss that case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t dismiss that case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But you’ve got to make an assessment, and this is the assessment we made.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Neil.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Hi, Chair Powell.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Neil Irwin, with Axios.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: So this has come up a couple of times today, but to be clear, do you believe that we’re experiencing a positive productivity shock, whether from AI or policy factors or whatever?

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: And how much of that is—how much is that driving the higher GDP projection in the SEP?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, yeah, I mean, I never thought I would see a time when we had, you know, five, six years of 2 percent productivity growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, this is definitely higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it was—before, it could be attributed to AI.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think you—I also think if you look at what AI can do and if you use it in your personal life, as I imagine many of us have, you can see the prospects for productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think it makes people who use it more productive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It may make other people have to find other jobs, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it could have productivity implications while also having, you know, social and labor market implications that we don’t have the tools to deal with.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, yes, I think we are seeing—we’re definitely seeing higher productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t—I think it’s a little quick to be saying it’s generative AI.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I don’t know—you know, the pandemic may have induced people to do more automation and do more things with computers to replace people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that raises productivity, you know, output per hour.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Does that imply a higher—does that imply a higher neutral rate and, therefore, the policy might be a little easier than it seems?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: All—you know, all things equal, yes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But all things aren’t equal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are many, many things pushing in different directions on where the neutral rate would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, yes, that argument does come up.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Matt Egan.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Thanks, Chair Powell.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Matt Egan, with CNN.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: After today, you only have three more meetings at the helm of the Fed.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Since becoming Fed Chair, you’ve seen multiple trade wars, the pandemic, COVID reopening, a period of high inflation.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: I know your term’s not up as Chair until May, but I’m wondering if you’ve given any thought to what you want your legacy to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My legacy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I—my thought is that I really want to turn this job over to whoever replaces me in—with the economy in really good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what I want to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I want inflation to be under control, coming back down to 2 percent, and I want the labor market to be strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what I want.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And all of my efforts are to get to that place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They have been all along, but, ultimately, that’s what I want.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s—you know, I don’t have time to think about bigger things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I have, I hope, many years ahead to worry about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But there’s enough to do.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Relatedly, have you given any more thought and can you tell us any more about your plans on whether or not you plan to stay on the Fed Board of Governors even after your term as Chair expires?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, I’m focused on—I’m focused on my remaining time as Chair.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I haven’t got anything new on that to tell you.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Mark for the last question.

speaker: MARK HAMRICK
sentence: Chairman, Mark Hamrick, with Bankrate.

speaker: MARK HAMRICK
sentence: Even while many price levels remain elevated, the reductions in the federal funds rate means that savings rates—or yields, to be more precise—have peaked, while key borrowing rates remain elevated.

speaker: MARK HAMRICK
sentence: And that’s, as we’ve discussed here, as many Americans struggle with liquidity or emergency savings challenges.

speaker: MARK HAMRICK
sentence: Is that just collateral damage or an unintended consequence because your tools are limited in addressing individual or household liquidity constraints, insufficient money in the bank?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would—I wouldn’t agree that that’s collateral damage of our—I mean, over time, we do what we do in order to create price stability and maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And those things are hugely valuable to all of the people we serve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: When we raise rates to bring inflation down, you know, that does work by slowing the economy, but we’ve moved back our rate—our policy back down to where it’s not—it’s certainly not strongly restrictive at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think it’s sort of in the range of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what we’re trying to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I would want people to understand that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think what people are feeling is the effect of higher prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There was a global wave, sort of every large economy in the world—sort of every large open economy, market-based economy in the world had a wave of inflation that looked an awful lot like ours.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We actually came through better than any other country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Substantially better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We had higher growth, we had a better labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And this is really due to the American economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have an extraordinary economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, people are innovative, they work hard.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so, you know, all of us who work in economics jobs are really fortunate to have the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So thank you very much.
